extracted.intended_audience: readers and historians of 19th-century American Catholic missions and religious communities
extracted.subtask_description: Biographical account of a Catholic missionary/founder (Rev. Charles Nerinckx) and the founding and conduct of associated religious communities in early-19th-century America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monastery conduct: poverty, simplicity, and separation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Have it all in a monastery-like manner as much as possible, poor with the bare necessities, out of sight, and separate as far as you can. Beware of elegancy, be satisfied with simplest everywhere except in your chapel, where extreme neatness — still no mundanity, that is, no worldly vanity or levity — ought to be found.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction from Father Nerinckx to the sisters prescribing austerity in daily life, avoidance of worldly elegance, secrecy/seclusion, and an exception of care/cleanliness in the chapel while avoiding worldly vanity. Emphasis on humility and mortification as normative virtues for the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily regimen and austerity of religious life
rubrics_metrics.description: The sisters’ life: perpetual silence (with one hour's recreation after dinner), frequent prayer, rising at four a.m., singing canticles while working, going barefoot, making their own dresses, sleeping upon a straw tick on the bare floor, and abstaining from coffee, tea, or sugar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed behavioral and material standards for community life — strict schedule, manual labor integrated with devotion, extreme simplicity of dress and diet — presented as exemplary and edifying, comparable to strict European foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency as basis for establishing houses
rubrics_metrics.description: “To establish them, it is enough to give them a piece of land, a hut, some farming implements, kitchen utensils, and looms; with these they themselves provide for all their wants, and find the means of giving a solid education to the children, in return for a few provisions furnished by the parents. They even take upon themselves the gratuitous care of destitute orphans.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for founding sisters’ houses in frontier contexts: minimal material endowment required, expectation of economic self-support through work, and role expectation to provide education and charitable care (orphan care) as part of mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community expansion judged by increase in scholars and members
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative observation that establishments were 'numerously attended by boarders and day-scholars, and increase in community members with a marvelous rapidity' and that reception of orphans and growth in scholars was an augury for the establishment's future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit success metrics for a mission/convent: growth in pupil enrollment and increases in community membership (including taking orphans) signal effective establishment and future stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural and material adequacy for chapel and convent
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on providing a chapel and adequate domestic structures (rooms fitted for school and chapel, frame church construction) despite poverty; examples include building a chapel, rooms for school and chapel, and later a large frame church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance that even austere communities should prioritize having a proper chapel and sufficient school/church structures; attention to physical arrangements (proximity to a spring, site selection near parish church) is practical guidance for establishing houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule legitimacy and canonical approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Father Nerinckx opposed local alterations of the Society's rules, noting that 'these rules, as already mitigated, had been approved of by the sacred congregation of the Propaganda, and indorsed by His Holiness, Pius VII.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard that community rules ought not be locally altered without regard to prior approval by appropriate ecclesiastical authorities; canonical endorsement (Propaganda, Pope) constitutes legitimacy and restraint on local modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral/administrative conduct: avoid meddling and refer local matters to the bishop
rubrics_metrics.description: Father Nerinckx 'avoided, as much as possible, meddling with the affairs of the branch houses, and invariably referred to the Bishop the local superiors who consulted him on temporal or spiritual matters concerning the direction of their community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive guideline for a founder or central director: refrain from over-involvement in branch-house administration; defer local temporal and spiritual disputes to the diocesan bishop to avoid clashes and division.
